newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian Duma says it puts off anti-Yeltsin move.
newsitem.headline: Russian Duma says it puts off anti-Yeltsin move.

text.p: The Russian parliament's press service said the State Duma agreed on Wednesday to postpone a final vote on a motion to remove President Boris Yeltsin on health grounds to give deputies time for more discussion.
But there was confusion over whether this was entirely what the deputies wanted, after some legislators admitted to reporters afterwards they had understood the voting differently.

The lower house first voted 229 to 63 for a communist motion "in principle", calling for Yeltsin's term to be declared ended on health grounds and for new presidential elections. Many government supporters boycotted the debate altogether.
The resolution's sponsor, Viktor Ilyukhin, then called for deputies to be given more time to discuss the move in their constituencies before coming back for a "definitive" vote in February.
A liberal deputy, Mikhail Yuriyev, countered that by urging the house to vote right away.

Pro-government deputy speaker Alexander Shokhin, who chaired the seven-hour debate, then, according to the parliamentary record, told the rowdy chamber to vote on the motion: "Who is for the proposal of deputy Yuriyev to hold a final vote?"
The house rejected that motion by 102 to 87 and Shokhin immediately closed the session.
Leaving the chamber, he told reporters that the deputies had finally rejected Ilyukhin's resolution on removing the president.
"That's it," he said. "If they want, they will have to start the whole thing over again from scratch."

However, some time later, a Duma spokesman told reporters the official record showed that what deputies had, in fact, rejected was simply Yuriyev's technical motion to hold an immediate vote. The house would, therefore, return to Ilyukhin's resolution for a final vote next month.

Some deputies admitted to reporters that they had misunderstood Shokhin's final call to vote. At least one said he had heard only part of the deputy speaker's call to vote and thought he was indeed voting on Ilyukhin's anti-Yeltsin resolution itself, not on Yuriyev's technical move.
It was not clear whether the Duma would return to the issue earlier than February.
The lower house's own legal department ruled that the resolution had no legal basis. Under the constitution, there is no clear mechanism for removing a sick president.
Government supporters had dismissed the communist move as frivolous and a threat to the stability of the state.
